title: Drag (physics)
description: Retarding force on a body moving in a fluid
wiki_lead:
In fluid dynamics, drag, sometimes referred to as fluid resistance, and also known as viscous force, is a force acting opposite to the direction of motion of any object moving with respect to a surrounding fluid. This can exist between two fluid layers, or between a fluid and a solid surface. Drag forces tend to decrease fluid velocity relative to the solid object in the fluid's path.
Unlike other resistive forces, drag force depends on velocity. Drag force is proportional to the relative velocity for low-speed flow and is proportional to the velocity squared for high-speed flow. This distinction between low and high-speed flow is measured by the Reynolds number.
wiki_excerpt:
In fluid dynamics, drag, sometimes referred to as fluid resistance, and also known as viscous force, is a force acting opposite to the direction of motion of any object moving with respect to a surrounding fluid. This can exist between two fluid layers, or between a fluid and a solid surface. Drag forces tend to decrease fluid velocity relative to the solid object in the fluid's path.
Unlike other resistive forces, drag force depends on velocity. Drag force is proportional to the relative velocity for low-speed flow and is proportional to the velocity squared for high-speed flow. This distinction between low and high-speed flow is measured by the Reynolds number.


Examples
Examples of drag include:

Net aerodynamic or hydrodynamic force: Drag acting opposite to the direction of movement of a solid object such as cars, aircraft, and boat hulls.
Viscous drag of fluid in a pipe: Drag force on the immobile pipe restricts the velocity of the fluid through the pipe.
In the physics of sports, drag force is necessary to explain the motion of balls, javelins, arrows, and frisbees and the performance of runners and swimmers. For a top sprinter, overcoming drag can require 5% of their energy output.


Types
There are many distinct types of drag caused by different physical interactions between the object and fluid. Two types of drag are relevant for all objects:

Form drag, which is caused by the pressure exerted on the object as the fluid flow goes around the object. Form drag is determined by the cross-sectional shape and area of the body.
Skin friction drag (or viscous drag), which is caused by friction between the fluid and the surface of the object. The surface may be the outside of an object, such as a boat hull, or the inside of an object, such as the bore of a pipe.
There are two types of which are primarily relevant for aircraft: 

Lift-induced drag appears with wings or a lifting body in aviation and with semi-planing or planing hulls for watercraft
Wave drag (aerodynamics) is caused by the presence of shockwaves and first appears at subsonic aircraft speeds when local flow velocities become supersonic. The wave drag of the supersonic Concorde prototype aircraft was reduced at Mach 2 by 1.8% by applying the area rule which extended the rear fuselage 3.73 m (12.2 ft) on the production aircraft.
Wave resistance affects watercraft:

Wave resistance (ship hydrodynamics) occurs when a solid object is moving along a fluid boundary and making surface waves.
Last, in aerodynamics the term "parasitic drag" is often used. Parasitic drag is the sum of form drag and skin friction drag and is entirely negative to an aircraft, in contrast with lift-induced drag which is a consequence of generating lift.

Lift-induced drag

Lift-induced drag (also called induced drag) is drag which occurs as the result of the creation of lift on a three-dimensional lifting body, such as the wing or propeller of an airplane. grok_lead: In physics, drag is the resistive force exerted by a fluid medium, such as air or water, on an object moving relative to it, acting in the direction opposite to the object's velocity. This force originates from the interactions between the object and the fluid's molecules, involving momentum transfer and pressure differences that impede motion. Drag is a fundamental concept in fluid dynamics, influencing the motion of everything from falling raindrops to high-speed aircraft, and its effects become prominent when objects move through dense fluids at appreciable speeds. The magnitude of the drag force is quantified by the drag equation: $ F_d = \frac{1}{2} C_d \rho A v^2 $, where $ C_d $ is the dimensionless drag coefficient (typically ranging from 0.1 for streamlined shapes to over 1 for blunt objects), $ \rho $ is the fluid's density, $ A $ is the object's cross-sectional area perpendicular to the flow, and $ v $ is the relative velocity. This quadratic dependence on velocity applies to high-speed flows (high Reynolds number s), while in low-speed, viscous-dominated regimes (low Reynolds number s), drag follows Stokes' law for spherical objects: $ F_d = 6\pi \eta r v $, where $ \eta $ is the fluid's viscosity and $ r $ is the sphere's radius. The Reynolds number, $ Re = \frac{\rho v L}{\eta} $ (with $ L $ as a characteristic length), determines the flow regime and thus the appropriate drag model, transitioning from linear to quadratic behavior as $ Re $ increases beyond approximately 1. Drag can be categorized into primary components: skin friction drag, arising from viscous shear stresses along the object's surface, and form (or pressure) drag, resulting from asymmetric pressure distributions due to flow separation around the object. In specialized contexts like aeronautics, additional types include induced drag (from lift generation) and wave drag (from compressibility effects at supersonic speeds), though these build on the core viscous and pressure mechanisms. The drag coefficient $ C_d $ encapsulates these effects and is often obtained through wind tunnel experiments or computational fluid dynamics simulations, varying with shape, surface roughness, and flow conditions. Understanding and mitigating drag is essential in engineering fields such as aerospace, automotive design, and marine propulsion, where reducing it improves fuel efficiency and performance; for instance, streamlining vehicle shapes can lower $ C_d $ by up to 50% compared to blunt forms. In natural phenomena, drag governs terminal velocities in free fall, limiting speeds of skydivers to about 53 m/s and raindrops to 9 m/s, balancing gravitational force against fluid resistance. Ongoing research refines drag models for complex geometries and turbulent flows, aiding advancements in sustainable transportation and environmental fluid mechanics.
